records.our_prose: Garlic grows fine in a deep pot because its roots are not huge. Use a container at least 8 inches deep with drainage holes, plant cloves 4 to 6 inches apart in fall, and plan to leave it out all winter. Keep it watered in spring and stop a couple of weeks before harvest.
records.source_context: Use the largest cloves for planting because larger cloves will yield larger bulbs. Plant cloves 4 to 6 inches apart and 1 to 2 inches deep, with the root side down and the pointy tip up. Fertilize once after planting and again when the weather warms up in the spring.

records.our_prose: Garlic is workable in containers given depth and drainage. Use a pot at least 8 inches deep, 3 gallons or more, set cloves 4 to 6 inches apart in fall, and treat it as a year-long resident: it overwinters in the pot and matures the next summer. Containers dry fast in spring, so water steadily through bulbing, then cut water two weeks before harvest. The main risk is winter waterlogging in a pot that drains poorly.

records.our_prose: Garlic (Allium sativum) is a hardy allium grown from individual cloves planted in fall. It roots before winter, overwinters in the ground (mulched in cold regions), then resumes growth in spring and matures the following summer, an eight to nine month crop that spans the year. Winter cold is essential: cloves must be vernalized to divide and bulb properly, which is why fall planting beats spring. Hardneck types suit cold winters, produce edible scapes, and store a few months; softneck types suit mild climates, braid well, and store the longest.

records.source_context: Fertilization In addition to the fertilizer used at planting, garlic needs additional nitrogen fertilizer to produce optimum yields. Side-dress with ½ pounds of nitrogen fertilizer (21-0-0) per 100 square feet in midApril and ¼ pounds in late May. Mulches Organic mulches help conserve water, supply extra nutrients and reduce weeding.

records.our_prose: Garlic has a moderate to high nitrogen demand and builds its bulb on the leaves it grows in spring, so feeding is front-loaded onto the spring vegetative push. Mix a complete fertilizer or compost into the bed at fall planting, then side-dress nitrogen as the shoots resume growth in early spring and again two to three weeks later. The exact cutoff tracks your season rather than a fixed calendar date. In cold-winter regions with a later crop, the last feedings run later: Utah State suggests about half a pound of 21-0-0 per 100 square feet in mid-April with a quarter pound in late May, and the University of Minnesota feeds through spring growth before bulbing. In the warm Southeast, where the crop runs weeks earlier, UGA advises no nitrogen after the first week of April. The unifying rule is to stop nitrogen several weeks before bulbing begins, since late feeding delays bulbing, thickens necks, and worsens storage.

records.our_prose: In the Arizona low desert, plant garlic in fall (September to November) and harvest in late spring or early summer, before the extreme heat. Garlic needs a few weeks of cool weather after planting to form a good bulb, so grow softneck types, and chilling the cloves in the fridge first helps in warm winters.

records.source_context: Plant Development Matured garlic cloves planted in the fall go through a dormant period. Garlic cloves require a period of 6–8 weeks of cool weather after planting (below 40 °F) to undergo vernalization (subjected to sufficient cold in order to induce bulbing) by low winter temperatures.
